heTitleNote: Shabbat day, at the second meal
progression: | Am Am | Dm Am | E E | Am Am |
metaLine: 100 BPM · 4/4 · sung at Shabbat lunch · six stanzas of four short lines, and every line in a stanza rhymes with the others
intro: The oldest song on this site: Dunash ben Labrat wrote it in tenth-century Spain, and he is the man who introduced Arabic quantitative metre into Hebrew poetry, which is why it scans the way it does. Six stanzas of four short lines, each stanza rhyming on one sound throughout, and the first letters spell the poet's name. It is sung at Shabbat lunch, quickly, and most tables get through three stanzas before the food arrives.

stanzas.label: freedom

lines.en: He will proclaim freedom for son and for daughter,
and He will keep you as the pupil of the eye.
Pleasant is your name, and it will not cease.
Sit, rest, on the Sabbath day.

stanzas.summary: Four lines, one rhyme: {{0.4}}, {{1.2}}, {{2.3}}, {{3.3}} all end in -at. That is the whole formal principle of the poem, and it is why it is so easy to learn — if a line does not rhyme, you have the wrong line. {{1.2}} is literally "like the pupil of the eye", the same image as in Deuteronomy 32.

stanzas.label: seek my sanctuary

lines.en: Seek out my sanctuary and my hall,
and make a sign of deliverance with me.
Plant a choice vine within my vineyard;
hear the cry of the children of my people.

stanzas.summary: {{6.1}} is a choice vine, the word Isaiah uses in the song of the vineyard. It is worth naming because a modern reader is likely to have met the same consonants as the name of a desalination plant — the site's own verified glossary offers exactly that reading, which is right for a lesson on modern Israel and wrong by a thousand years here.

stanzas.label: tread the winepress

lines.en: Tread the winepress within Botzrah,
and Babylon too, which grew strong.
Shatter my oppressors in anger and fury;
hear my voice on the day I call.

stanzas.summary: The winepress and Botzrah are Isaiah 63, where the image is judgement rather than harvest. {{11.0}} is the imperative of the verb in the Shema — the same word a learner meets on day one of the prayer book, here doing something quite different.

stanzas.label: in the wilderness

lines.en: God, set in the wilderness a mountain —
myrtle, acacia, cypress and box tree —
and to the one who warns and the one who is warned,
glosses: and to the one who warns
and to the one who heeds warning

lines.en: give peace like the waters of a river.

stanzas.summary: The four trees are Isaiah 41, a list of what will grow where nothing grew. {{14.0}} and {{14.1}} are the same root in two voices — the one who warns and the one who is warned — and the poem asks for peace for both of them, which is more generous than it first sounds.

stanzas.label: put down my adversaries

lines.en: Crush those who rise against me, jealous living God,
with melting of heart and with breaking;
and we will open wide our mouth and fill it,
our tongue is a song of joy to You.

stanzas.summary: {{18.0}} and {{18.2}} are a quotation of Psalm 81 — open your mouth wide and I will fill it — turned from a promise into a resolution. The poem takes a line God says and gives it to the singer.

stanzas.label: know wisdom

lines.en: Know wisdom, for your own soul,
and she is a crown for your head.
Keep the commandment of your Holy One;
guard your holy Sabbath.

stanzas.summary: The last stanza is the only one addressed to the singer rather than to God, and it is the only one that mentions the Sabbath again after the first. The poem opens with rest commanded and closes with rest kept.

chantTips: Sung at Shabbat lunch, briskly, and often not to the end. Three stanzas is a normal amount.
Each stanza has its own rhyme sound and it never varies within the stanza. If you are learning by ear, that rhyme is your handrail.
The lines are short — three or four words — so the melody turns around quickly. Do not stretch them.
There are several tunes in circulation, including one that borrows a well-known secular melody. Whichever the table starts, join it.

about.body: Tenth century, North Africa and then Córdoba, and the poet who brought Arabic quantitative metre into Hebrew verse. That importation is the reason Hebrew poetry sounds the way it does for the next five hundred years, and this table song is one of the few pieces of his that everyone still sings.

The first letters of the stanzas spell the poet's name. The sixth stanza is generally taken to be a later addition, since it falls outside that acrostic — the same situation as the last stanza of Maoz Tzur, and it is printed here for the same reason.

about.h: Almost every line is a quotation
about.body: Deuteronomy, Isaiah twice, Psalms. None of them is marked. A piyyut of this period assumes a listener who has the Tanakh by heart, and it builds a new poem out of half-lines the audience will recognise as they pass.

The Hebrew here is Daat Siddur Ashkenaz, public domain, via Sefaria and pinned in this repository. That edition marks four alternative readings and closes with an attribution to the poet; the scaffold removed all five rather than printing them as lines to be sung, and lists each one when it runs.
